source_sections: Definition Bell number number of partitions of n-element set

contexts.context: Bell number indexed by any nonnegative integer counts set partitions

forms.label: count-partitions
forms.text: For n∈ℕ₀, the Bell number B_n is the number of distinct partitions of any set S with |S|=n into nonempty pairwise disjoint blocks whose union is S; in particular B_0=1.

review: ProofWiki directly defines Bell number B_n by counting partitions of an n-element set and explicitly lists B_0=1. This is well defined for each nonnegative integer because the count depends only on the set cardinality: bijections between n-element sets transport partitions. The empty set has exactly one partition, the empty collection of blocks, so B_0=1 and not 0. An unindexed partition is a collection of distinct nonempty blocks, not an ordered list or arbitrary indexed tuple; ordering blocks overcounts Bell numbers. The Bell number counts partitions with ANY number of blocks, unlike the Stirling number of the second kind S(n,k) counting exactly k blocks. The source sequence is nonnegative integers B_n; no analytic Bell-function extension or other Bell-number senses assumed. The earlier independently screened partition-of-set meaning fixes the nonempty-block convention.

term: Stirling numbers of the second kind
source_sections: Definition 1 Kronecker delta boundary and recurrence
Number of Set Partitions by Number of Components independently corroborated

contexts.context: Stirling numbers S(n,k) with n,k nonnegative integers, two equivalent defining characterizations

forms.label: recursion-with-boundary
forms.text: For n,k∈ℕ₀, the Stirling numbers of the second kind S(n,k) satisfy S(n,0)=δ_{n,0}, S(0,k)=δ_{0,k}, and for n,k≥1, S(n,k)=S(n−1,k−1)+k S(n−1,k), where δ is Kronecker's delta.

forms.label: falling-factorial-basis-coefficients
forms.text: For each n∈ℕ₀, the Stirling numbers S(n,k) are the unique coefficients in the polynomial identity x^n=∑_{k=0}^n S(n,k)x^{\underline{k}}, where x^{\underline{0}}=1 and x^{\underline{k}}=x(x−1)⋯(x−k+1) for k≥1.

review: ProofWiki directly gives recurrence S(n,k)=S(n−1,k−1)+kS(n−1,k) with Kronecker-delta boundary when n=0 or k=0, and the falling-factorial polynomial coefficient characterization. These two describe the SAME family of nonnegative-integer-indexed Stirling numbers of the second kind, not two unrelated objects. Independently checked its Number of Set Partitions by Number of Components theorem: S(n,k) counts partitions of an n-element set into k blocks, including S(0,0)=1; no third source-form observation is asserted for that theorem in this initial intake. Boundary S(n,0)=δ_{n,0} rules out nonempty-set zero-block partitions. Polynomial identity explicitly uses k=0 to n; falling factorial is x(x−1)...(x−k+1) for positive k and 1 at k=0. Uniqueness follows because falling factorial polynomials form a monic graded basis. No Stirling numbers of the FIRST kind or signed/unsigned variants are merged. No complex-variable extension is imposed because the equality is a polynomial identity and can be interpreted symbolically.

term: convex hull of a subset of a real vector space
source_sections: Definition 1 all finite strictly positive coefficient convex combinations
Equivalence of Definitions of Convex Hull checked

contexts.context: Convex hull of subset U of a real vector space V, three equivalent set constructions

forms.label: finite-convex-combinations
forms.text: For a real vector space V and U⊆V, conv(U) is the set of sums ∑_{j=1}^m λ_j u_j with m≥1, u_j∈U, λ_j>0 for all j, and ∑_{j=1}^m λ_j=1; conv(∅)=∅.

forms.label: intersection-convex-supersets
forms.text: For a real vector space V and U⊆V, conv(U)=⋂{C⊆V:C is convex and U⊆C}, the intersection of every convex subset containing U.

forms.label: least-convex-superset
forms.text: For a real vector space V and U⊆V, conv(U) is the unique least (by inclusion) convex subset C⊆V with U⊆C; every convex D containing U contains C.

review: ProofWiki directly lists THREE equivalent descriptions: all finite strictly positive-weight convex combinations of elements of U, intersection of all convex sets containing U, and smallest convex superset. The source additionally has a separate equivalence-of-definitions theorem which was read. These all describe ONE convex hull meaning in a REAL vector space V, for ANY subset U (including empty U), not a closed convex hull, affine hull, or linear span. Positive weights are harmless compared with nonnegative finite convex combinations because terms with zero weight may be discarded; m≥1 means no nonempty convex combination exists for empty U, so conv(∅)=∅. Empty subset is conventionally convex, so intersection of convex supersets for U=∅ also equals ∅, consistent with the finite-combination definition. The convex subset predicate itself is separately needed to fully link formulations 2 and 3; no source-screened target should be invented before discovery. Convex hull need not be closed in infinite-dimensional normed spaces, so closed convex hull is DIFFERENT. Convex combinations are finite, not general countably infinite sums. The least-convex-superset condition is inclusion-minimal plus contained in every convex superset, not any arbitrary minimal convex superset.

term: degree of a vertex in a simple undirected graph
source_sections: Definition number of edges incident to vertex
Source examples for loops and multigraphs require a different counting convention

contexts.context: Degree of vertex in a loopless simple undirected graph, incidence and neighbor cardinality equivalent

forms.label: incident-edge-cardinality
forms.text: For a simple undirected graph G=(V,E) and v∈V, deg_G(v) is the cardinality of the set {e∈E:v∈e} of edges incident to v.

forms.label: adjacent-vertex-cardinality
forms.text: For a simple undirected graph G=(V,E) and v∈V, deg_G(v)=|{u∈V:{u,v}∈E}|, the number or cardinality of distinct vertices adjacent to v.

review: ProofWiki defines vertex degree as the number of incident edges and immediately equates it to number of distinct neighbors, which is correct for a SIMPLE UNDIRECTED LOOPLESS graph, since each neighbor corresponds bijectively to exactly one incident edge. However the same source later discusses loop multigraph examples, where these two counting expressions are NOT equivalent: parallel edges give multiple incident edges but one neighboring vertex, and graph loop edges usually count twice in degree, not once. Thus both forms are accepted only in the explicitly specialized simple-graph context, and their extension to multigraphs is NOT promoted. No finiteness is required: degree can be an infinite cardinal if V is infinite. An isolated vertex has degree zero. For a finite simple graph the number of neighbors is a nonnegative integer, but the more general cardinality is valid here. This source issue is a contextual overgeneralization, not a new universal mathematical equivalence.
